picture: RimWorld, a small colony at dusk. A raid letter. A short fight at the door; one colonist falls. Cut to three days later: the cook drops her work and walks out into the fields. The player clicks her. The needs tab fills the screen, every mood effect a line with a number and a timer.
Title card over the game-by-mechanic grid, out of focus.
The paused colony. RimWorld's core mechanics peel off the screen as labelled cards: storyteller, needs, mood breaks, memories, work priorities, injuries by body part, threat that grows with wealth.
Four stamps land on the storyteller card.
Each core card flies to its column in the grid. Most columns are thin.
Arrows from three columns back to one row: Dwarf Fortress, 2006. Then a still of Façade: two characters at a dinner party.
The game-by-mechanic grid fills in row by row, oldest game at the top, a year counter ticking in the corner.

The grid narrows to its fullest columns. Five light up in turn, each over a two-second clip: a paused raid, a building dropped on a lot, a mod list, a research screen, a scenario goal. Then a sixth: ore riding a belt into a furnace.
Two histograms build side by side: the parts games call core, and the parts they call supporting, by how many games use each.
SimCity, 1989. A block of houses stalls next to an industrial strip. The crime map washes over it, then land value.
Factorio: a factory grows; a pollution cloud spreads chunk by chunk; biters leave their nests.
Oxygen Not Included: a temperature overlay; heat creeps out of a generator room into the base.
The Sims: a Sim heads to the fridge on its own; the bills sit unpaid until the player clicks.
A table builds row by row: each subgenre, and the three families of parts it uses most.
A blank grid row with a cursor over it.

A teletype printing on paper. A steward's yearly report scrolls up: people starved, people arrived, bushels per acre, bushels eaten by rats, the price of land. A cursor blinks after a question about how many acres to plant.
The player types an answer. The next report says a plague has struck and half the people are dead. Hard cut to black.
Title card over the stacked chart of the vocabulary, out of focus.
Hamurabi's six mechanics peel off the terminal as labelled cards: crops, random disasters, consumption, turns, spoilage, an advisor.

scene_title: A date is an upper bound
picture: A timeline. Each mechanic card drops onto the year of its first catalog game. Then a second, faded track appears above the first, labelled "outside the catalog": a mainframe program, a book cover, two board games, a Minecraft mod.
The stacked chart builds year by year, one coloured layer per family, oldest families at the bottom. Two years spike: 1989 and 2013.

Thirty-seven cards shuffle out of the full catalog at random, then shrink to the sizes of the early games. A counter tallies the mechanics they cover. The shuffle repeats, fast, and a histogram of counts builds up. A marker shows where the real early games land.
SimCity, 1989. The land value overlay washes over the map, then crime, then pollution. A line of the Micropolis source code fades in over the crime map.
M.U.L.E., 1983. Four players walk their avatars toward a price line in a live auction for smithore.
Little Computer People, 1985. A small man in a cross-section of a three-storey house reads a typed request and shakes his head.
Elite, 1984: a wireframe ship docks at a rotating station; the galaxy map shows hundreds of named systems.
Theme Park, 1994: a crowd of visitors, each with a thought bubble; one walks past a ride with a long queue toward a shop.
A Tale in the Desert: a crowd of player avatars around a voting monument. Then EVE Online's market screen, columns of buy and sell orders.
Dwarf Fortress. A miner breaches a cavern wall; water pours tile by tile down a corridor and fills a workshop level by level.
Factorio: a belt of iron ore splits into two lanes and feeds a row of furnaces. Then Papers, Please: a passport stamped DENIED. Then BeamNG.drive: a car's frame folds against a pole.
The Oregon Trail: a supply screen with food, clothing, and medicine counters ticking down. Match cut to Minecraft's hunger bar draining.
Stardew Valley, a spring morning: the energy bar full, a field of parsnips, a villager's heart meter. Each part gets a small date tag as it appears: 1968, 1993, 1996, 1996, 1997.
Factorio's core parts lay out as date tags: 1982, 1983, 1989, 1991, 1998, 2006, and one tag reading 2013 on the conveyor belt.
A blank list with a year column beside it.
The design map of the catalog fades in, islands of games, with Factorio and Anno 1800 highlighted on different islands.
Factorio at night. A row of assemblers slows; the power graph shows demand above supply. Pollution clouds drift over a forest toward a nest of biters, which stir.
Anno 1800 by day. A street of artisans' houses with a needs panel open: canned food missing. A cargo ship crawls across the sea between two islands.
Title card over the design map of the catalog, islands of games, out of focus.
Factorio's mechanics on the left as cards, Anno's on the right. Six cards slide to the middle: production chains, storage, building placement, blueprints, vehicle routes, a late-game megaproject.

The cards left on each side light up: belts, power grid, pollution, evolving enemies, circuits on the left; population tiers, consumption per house, trade between islands, rival companies on the right.
Every game in the catalog becomes a bundle of cards. Common cards, like the pause button, shrink almost to nothing; rare cards grow. Bundles with similar large cards drift together into clumps.

The catalog drops a fifth of its games at random, re-clusters, and compares the result with the full clustering. A score ticks up and down. The process repeats, fast, a thousand times. A curve of average agreement against the number of clusters draws itself, nearly flat on the right.
Split screen. Left: Papers, Please, a passport under a lamp, a rulebook page, a clock. Right: Princess Maker 2, a month's calendar split into three slots, a daughter's attribute chart.
Job Simulator in VR: a hand throws a stapler across an office cubicle. Cut to Besiege: a wooden siege engine flips itself over.
Farming Simulator 25: a combine harvester working a field in a straight GPS line. Cut to iRacing: a car in a pit lane.
Black & White: a giant creature being slapped for eating a villager. Cut to Creatures: a Norn being tickled.
Europa Universalis IV's map in political colours. Cut to Tropico 6: El Presidente on a balcony, a faction approval panel.
Theme Hospital: a corridor of patients with thought bubbles; a hiring screen of doctors.
RimWorld's colony and The Sims' house, side by side.
inZOI: a character in a kitchen with a thought line written in plain sentences. Cut to AI Dungeon: a column of generated story text.
Elite, 1984, a wireframe ship. Dissolve to Elite Dangerous, 2014, the same docking manoeuvre in full colour.
M.U.L.E.'s auction screen. Dissolve to Offworld Trading Company's market panel, prices moving with each sale.
Frostpunk: a radial city around a glowing generator, temperature dropping on a gauge, the Book of Laws open on child labour.
Frostpunk 2: a council chamber, a hundred seats coloured by faction, a vote count climbing toward 51.
The design map with each game coloured by its store genre. Most islands are mostly one colour; many have a second and third.
The Game of Life's glider crawling across a grid, next to Hamurabi's text report.
A blank card bundle for the viewer's game, with its rare parts circled.
The colony-sim island zooms in: RimWorld and Dwarf Fortress side by side, a mood panel on one and a legends screen on the other.

Dwarf Fortress, side view of a fortress three levels deep. A miner cuts the last tile of a tunnel to the river. Water spills down the tunnel, fills a cistern, and keeps coming: down a stairwell, across the dining hall, into a row of bedrooms. Depth numbers flicker on the flooded tiles, one to seven.
Title card over a still of the flooded dining hall.

The water pumped out, dwarves back at work. A dwarf's portrait with a meter beside it that the game never shows, labelled "stress (hidden)". The meter creeps up. Months pass on a calendar in the corner. The metalsmith throws a tantrum and smashes a table while the other dwarves watch.
A later game in the same world. Legends mode: the fortress listed as a site, the flood among its events. An adventurer walks into the dry, empty hall.
Two five-step scales slide in, each step labelled with its anchor text: legibility and emergence potential. Three mechanic cards drop onto them: stress, simulated history, the pause button.
A caption card.
The scatter of every mechanic, legibility across, emergence up, each dot sized by how many games use it. The dots settle into a cloud that leans down to the right.
The interface mechanics, overlays, tooltips, speed controls, light up in the bottom right corner, then fade out of the plot. The cloud still leans.

Conway's Game of Life in a simulator. The rule written across the top: born with 3 neighbors, survives with 2 or 3. A five-cell R-pentomino starts to grow and doesn't stop; a generation counter climbs past a thousand.
EVE Online: a market window with a price history chart, then a fleet battle, wrecks drifting.
RimWorld. A colony with gold statues and fine furniture; a raid letter; an enormous raid. Then the raid points formula builds on screen term by term.
Oxygen Not Included. A base in normal view, then the oxygen overlay washes over it: pockets of carbon dioxide where the duplicants are about to walk. Then the temperature overlay.
SimCity (1989), the traffic map: a heat map of density, no cars anywhere. Cut to Cities: Skylines, a jam forming at one intersection, cars stacked in one lane while the lane beside it is empty.

A montage of interface: SimCity's land value map, a Victoria 3 tooltip opening a second tooltip inside it, a RollerCoaster Tycoon guest window with a thought reading that a ride was too intense, Dwarf Fortress Legends scrolling.

Split screen: Dwarf Fortress on the left, RimWorld on the right. The same event on each side: a character breaking down. On the left, a dwarf storming about with no explanation on screen. On the right, a mood bar with its thresholds and a list of thoughts.
A blank sheet with a chain of boxes, each labelled "visible", "findable", or "hidden".

The Sims (2000). A Sim with a low Hunger bar. The player opens Buy mode; the clock stops. A new refrigerator goes against the kitchen wall. Time starts. The Sim turns away from the television, crosses the house, opens the refrigerator, and starts cooking.
Title card over the kitchen, frozen.
The kitchen again, with diagram labels popping off each object: refrigerator, Hunger; bed, Energy; toilet, Bladder 0 to 70. Lines run from the Sim to each label, thicker for the ones she needs most.
A row of five ceiling tiles above the kitchen, each labelled: authoring, compute, legibility, determinism, believability.

Crusader Kings III: an event window about a rival's illness; a few game months later, a follow-up event about the succession; then a war declaration. Cut to Reigns: cards swiped left and right, four meters at the top of the screen moving.
Façade: the couple at their dinner, a text box, the player typing. A diagram fans the typed sentence into a short list of labels: agree, criticize, flirt.
RimWorld late in a long game: a large colony, the speed set to fastest. A graphic overlay, added in the edit, reads the speed the game is actually managing; it falls below the speed on the button.
Noita: a pool of oil catches fire, steam bursts out of a flooded chamber, a ceiling of sand collapses. Every pixel moves.
SimCity (2013): agents carrying water and workers along the roads of a small city that stops at the edge of a tight boundary.
Callback: Dwarf Fortress's flooded dining hall, then RimWorld's list of thoughts.
Factorio: a belt of iron plates, items moving in exact single file. The camera pulls back to two players' screens side by side, the same factory, the same item at the same spot on the same belt.
RollerCoaster Tycoon: hundreds of guests on the paths. One is clicked; a thought reads that a ride is too intense. Then RimWorld: one colonist's thought list, long and specific.
Creatures (1996): a Norn being tickled, then slapped; a diagram of its brain, chemistry, and genome.
Figures from the Generative Agents paper: the small town, agents' speech bubbles, a diagram of word spreading from one agent to many.
The five ceiling tiles again. As each example is named, one tile lifts and another lowers.

A board with the five ceilings as columns and recent techniques as cards being pinned under them. Most cards pile up under authoring and rendering; one card, neural upscaling, is marked shipped everywhere.

Suck Up! A cartoon street at night. The player, a vampire in a delivery-driver disguise, knocks. A resident opens the door a crack. Subtitles show the player's spoken pitch and the resident's spoken reply: she isn't expecting a parcel. The door shuts. Cut to the same door, a new disguise. This time she steps aside.
Title card over the closed door.

scene_title: When the model is the game
picture: AI Dungeon, a text screen. The player types an action; a paragraph appears. Several turns later the player mentions a silver key. The story ignores it. The player opens the memory box and types the key in.
A four-step ladder: research, prototype, shipped in one game, shipped as a norm. Technique names drop onto the rungs, most of them landing on the bottom two.
Microsoft Flight Simulator, a low pass over a city. A split screen: rendered frames on the left, generated frames marked in between on the right.
Flight Simulator's camera pulls up from a street to a whole region, every roof and tree in place. Then inZOI: a photo dragged into a menu becomes a 3D lamp in a living room.

inZOI: the player types a thought into a prompt box, and a Zoi changes course across the room. Where Winds Meet: a player speaks to a market trader, who answers. Whispers from the Star: Stella on a video call, waiting for an answer.

A drawn top-down hairpin, labelled as a graphic: a car marked GT Sophy takes the inside line and holds it while a second car runs wide. Then two dated cards: February 2023, a limited event; November 2023, a permanent rival. No Gran Turismo 7 footage: Sony's licence bars broadcasting it without written consent (media/rights.yaml).
Townscaper: a click on the water adds a block, and arches, stairs, and roofs rearrange around it. Then a spreadsheet of level difficulty estimates with a column of agent pass rates.

The shipped techniques as cards, sorted into two piles: "changes what you see and hear" and "changes the game's state." The second pile has three cards: cached rules, characters that act, opponents. Then clips from world-model demos: a DOOM corridor generated frame by frame; a Genie 3 world where a character walks through a wall.
A replay timeline scrubbing back and forth. Model calls appear on it as small flags, each flag holding a stored answer.
Survey charts from GDC 2025 and 2026, two bars side by side. inZOI's Steam review graph dipping in May 2025.
The two piles of cards again. The "changes the game's state" pile is pushed forward; Infinite Craft's card is on top.

Infinite Craft. Four tiles: water, fire, wind, earth. The cursor drags one onto another; a new tile pops out. Faster now, combination after combination. Then one combination pauses for a beat, a new tile appears, and a badge flashes: First Discovery.
Title card over a wall of tiles.
A diagram: a pair of tiles goes into a lookup box. Hit: the stored answer comes back. Miss: an arrow to a model, then back into the box, which now holds one more row.
A timeline of the dataset's techniques by year: a thin trickle from 2006, then a wall of cards from 2023 on, most labelled with language models or world models.

Seven quick clips, each labelled with one effect: a Zoi crossing a room on a model's decision, "replaces"; a GT Sophy car on the limit, "deepens"; a teammate following a spoken order, "enables"; a scene appearing from a typed prompt, "cuts authoring"; a tooltip, "explains"; a bot running a test level, "tunes"; a flight sim at a higher frame rate, "accelerates."

RimWorld's needs tab, every thought listed with a number and a timer. Victoria 3: a tooltip, then a tooltip inside the tooltip, then another. Dwarf Fortress: a dwarf throwing a tantrum, with nothing on screen saying why.
The technique-flows figure builds: techniques on the left, effects in the middle, mechanic families on the right, ribbons running between them. Four families on the right collect most of the ribbons.
A ranked list builds: generative content, procedural terrain, utility action selection. Beside each, a small bar of how many catalog games use it. The first bar is tiny.

Crusader Kings III: an event window about a rival's illness, then a second event weeks later about a succession dispute. The Sims: a Sim choosing between a fridge, a bed, and a TV, each with a diagram score drawn above it.

Factorio. A long production line; one furnace far upstream sits idle while the player inspects an assembler at the end of the line. The family-exposure bars rearranged per mechanic, resources and logistics at the bottom.

A scatter of mechanics: judged AI leverage on one axis, exposure on the other. A handful of points sit high on judgment and flat on exposure, labelled: mod support, simulated history, blueprints, creature care.
The family bars again, the economic core dark at the bottom. Cut to a city at night with no events on screen.
Cities: Skylines. A tidy riverside district, built all at once. Time-lapse: decades pass. Hearses queue down the main road, house after house.
Title card over the queue of hearses.
Two columns of game covers. On the left, games with building placement; it's long. On the right, games with triggered event chains; it's short. One cover slides into the middle: Surviving Mars.
SimCity (1989). The land value overlay, then the traffic overlay, toggled back and forth over the same streets. Cut to Football Manager: a match engine highlight, then a board confidence screen.
The vacant-lots figure builds: mechanic names down a staircase, lots filling in where rows meet columns. Dark lots, dashed lots, a few slashed ones.
Banished: a village in winter, a family's house, a child who grows into a worker across a time-lapse. Then Captain of Industry and Workers & Resources: trucks, conveyors, smelters, and no faces.

SpaceChem: a solution finishes, and three histograms rise showing where it ranks against everyone else's. Factorio: a player copies a blueprint string out of the game. Spore: a creature browser, thousands of player-made animals.
Crusader Kings III: a court screen full of faces and opinions. Stellaris: three research cards, each with a scientist's portrait and traits.

Prison Architect: a guard walks past a generator room; a shared prison downloads; an Escape Mode prisoner slips out. Kenshi: a squad member with a missing arm hauls ore. Against the Storm: a new map unfolds for a new settlement.
Kerbal Space Program: a rocket assembled part by part in the hangar, then flown by hand off the pad.
A pull request on screen adding one game record. The build reruns; a sentence in the book turns red; it's rewritten.
The vacant-lots plan again, a handful of dashed lots outlined in colour.

Factorio, mid-game. The science counter ticks slowly. The production graph shows electronic circuits falling. The player places four new circuit assemblers and connects them; their input slots stay empty. The camera follows a belt upstream, past the cable assemblers, to a smelter column where one belt carries iron and copper together, the iron filling both lanes.
Title card over the ranked table of opportunities, out of focus.

scene_title: A tool that names the cause
picture: Mock-up, labelled: the same factory with a bottleneck view switched on. Machines shade from grey to orange by how much one more unit of each would raise circuit output. The cable assemblers glow. A one-line explanation appears with a link that jumps the camera to the shared belt.
The bottleneck explainer's record scrolls past, field by field: mechanics, techniques, precedent games, thesis, sketch, experiment, prediction.
Three dials, impact, feasibility, novelty, combine into one priority number. The ranked table builds.

Mock-up, labelled: a colony sim. The player right-clicks a closed hospital and picks "why?". Five sentences appear, each with a small link. Clicking one scrubs a timeline back to the event it names. A small causal graph draws beside the text.

Democracy 4, a policy screen. Mock-up, labelled: a Preview button. The view splits into a fan of faint lines for unemployment and approval over the next year, then two short replays of the futures that differ most.
RimWorld again. The cook from episode 1, walking out of the kitchen. Her needs tab. Mock-up, labelled: one new line in the list, referring to her son by name and to an argument the week before.

Mock-up, labelled: an in-game mod workshop. The player types "wolves avoid fire". A diff to the game's data and scripts appears, then a headless test map where wolves circle a campfire at a distance, then before-and-after numbers, then a Share button.

A diagram builds: a solid block labelled "simulation state" in the middle; around it, four arrows from outside labelled read, explain, decorate, propose; a gate labelled "validator" on the propose arrow; a strip labelled "log" along the bottom.

The bottom of the feasibility scale. Three record cards slide in. Mock-up stills, labelled: a city drawn as watercolor over a tile grid; a map of hundreds of small agents with a chronicle scrolling beside it.
The ranked table again, its rows sorting into three columns: small studio, engine and tools, research.
The Factorio factory from the cold open, running, the smelter belts split. The ranked table again, every row with a date beside it.

Animated diagram: two monitors side by side showing the same strategy map, an enemy cavalry unit in the middle. A small clock icon over each labelled "AI thinking time". On the left monitor the cavalry turns north; on the right it holds. Two checksums appear under the screens, different. A dialog box: "Desync".
Title card over the desync dialog, out of focus.
The dataset's record for Monte Carlo tree search, scrolling to its limitations. One line highlights.
Factorio multiplayer: two players' views of the same factory, belts moving in perfect step. Overlay: a replay file icon, a bug report icon, a leaderboard, a save file.
A diagram: a model's answer drops into a cache, and two players' screens read the same entry.
Townscaper: a player clicks along a waterline and houses, arches, and stairs assemble themselves.
A diagram of a first-person view where the player icon jumps, then jumps again in mid-air.
Victoria 3-style nested tooltips (diagram), each number opening into its causes. Then the same panel replaced by a single grey box labelled "learned policy", with nothing to open.
A stack of coins grows beside a clock labelled "player-hours". Then a timer counting down from sixty seconds over a blurred generated world.
The risk table from the dataset builds as a bar chart, longest bar at the top.
Plain text cards, one per fact, over a dark background.

The desync diagram from the cold open again. This time the opponent's move is computed once, written as a line in a scrolling log, and sent to both monitors. The checksums match. Then the same log feeds three small panels: a replay, a "why?" answer with links, and a forked timeline.
The two monitors from the cold open, in step, the match continuing.
A wall calendar flips to 31 December 2027. Index cards pin themselves to the date, one by one. The camera stops on the first card and reads it.
Title card over the predictions table, out of focus.
The prediction's record on screen. Its criteria highlight one clause at a time.
Mock-up: a generic strategy game's patch notes, "New: ask the Advisor anything". The checker clicks through to the details: answers come from the game's manual.
An early draft of a prediction, from the project's history, with three words circled: "major", "popular", "peer studio".
One opportunity record, split down the middle: on the left its validation experiment, on the right its prediction.
The predictions table scrolls, grouped by year. A bar under each year grows to its count.
Four prediction cards in a grid. Each one's limiting clause highlights as the narration reaches it.
The resolution brief on screen. Then a resolution block being added to a prediction's record: outcome, date, run, evidence, note.
The ranked table of bets, with an empty column labelled "outcome" beside it. Then the technique table, its maturity column highlighted: research, prototype, shipped in a niche, shipped as a norm.
A blank card with four numbered lines, filling in as the narration goes.
The calendar from the cold open, the cards still pinned to 31 December 2027.

A re-enactment of the run's terminal, labelled as one. An agent adds three game records, Pocket City, Fallout Shelter, Game Dev Story, and runs the dataset's checks. The data checks pass. Then a red line: a report assertion failed. The cursor stops on it.
Title card over a scrolling build log, out of focus.
The white-space table from episode 8. The row pairing building placement with embodied skill control highlights, then slides out of the table as a threshold line rises past it.
A folder tree: one YAML file per game, mechanic, technique, opportunity, and source, and a folder of run records. Arrows lead from the folder to the paper, the website, the book, and this script.
A sentence from episode 1 on screen, with its hidden tokens revealed beneath it: a stat, two ranks, an assertion.
The first version of the catalog grid beside the current one. In the old grid, the pause, placement, and tech tree columns are almost empty. In the new one they're the fullest on the board.
The design map from episode 3, islands of games. One game at a time blinks out; some island borders shift.
A run record on screen: id, kind, date, actor, operator, model, purpose, and a long method paragraph that includes what failed.
Two build folders side by side, every file name matching, a diff tool reporting no differences.
A record's status field cycling through asserted, sourced, verified. Then a still of Utopia on the Intellivision, with two dates beside it: 1981 and 1982.
A quote highlighted on a web page, a green check beside it. Then the same quote next to the claim it supports, with a question mark between them.
The repository's task list, issues labelled verify, rate, resolve. Then the game-by-mechanic grid from episode 1, filling in one more row.

A teletype prints a line of text in 1968: the steward's yearly report on a city's grain. The camera pulls back as the line becomes the first row of the catalog grid, and rows pour in beneath it, one per game, a year counter running in the corner up to 2026.
The grid's five fullest columns light up, then RimWorld's row with its core columns, each nearly empty.
The technique-flow ribbons draw in from the right and land on a handful of columns; most of the grid stays unlit.
A calendar strip scrolls forward; dates light up one by one, the first group bunched on a single day.

The five ceilings from episode 5 as five horizontal lines across the screen. Dots appear on a timeline beneath them, one per technique, each rising to the ceiling it presses on and colored by how far it has shipped.
The determinism line darkens as a cluster of dots pushes down on it from above.
The vacant-lots plan on the left half of the screen, the technique-flow ribbons on the right. Lines from both run to the middle and become the rows of one table.
The table sorts itself by priority; the top rows glow, then every row's status cell reads "open".
The catalog grid, every game a row and every mechanic a column, columns sorted by how many games use them. The five fullest columns light up left to right.

Two seconds per part, each labelled with its rank: RimWorld paused mid-raid; a building dropped onto an empty lot in Cities: Skylines; a mod list; Factorio's research screen; a RollerCoaster Tycoon scenario goal.
The sixth column lights up. Factorio: ore rides a belt into a furnace and comes out as plates.
The camera slides right along the grid to RimWorld's row. Its core columns light up, each one nearly empty.
Stardew Valley, a spring morning on the farm. Small date tags pop up over the crops, the energy bar, the calendar, and a villager's heart meter.
Each tag expands into a clip of its source: Hamurabi's green text report; Princess Maker 2's month split into three slots; Harvest Moon's seasonal calendar.
The catalog grid; rows for games since 2010 light up, and most of their marks turn the colour of pre-2000 parts.
Stardew Valley's friendship screen; a heart meter fills to one heart, then drains a little each day the player stays away.
Split screen. Left: a passport under a desk lamp in Papers, Please. Right: Princess Maker 2's daughter at her desk with a schedule.
The design map of the catalog; games drift into islands, the map reshuffles over and over, and the two games keep landing on the same island.
Side by side: the border shift clock and the month's three slots; the family ledger and the annual income; a scripted visitor and a festival announcement.
The Sims' family in a kitchen slides in, then slides off the island.
RimWorld. A gold statue is placed in the dining room.
The raid points formula builds term by term over the colony. A raid letter arrives; a long line of raiders crosses the map.
A plain stone colony: wooden stools, bare floors, a narrow corridor of turrets at the gate.
The game screen, with no raid number anywhere. Then the community wiki page with the formula.
The Sims (2000). A hungry Sim walks across the house to a refrigerator and starts cooking.
Diagram labels pop off each object in the house: refrigerator, Hunger; bed, Energy. Lines run from the Sim to each label, thickest to the one she needs most.
New objects pour into the Buy mode catalog, each one bringing a new action into the Sim's menu.
The Buy catalog scrolls and scrolls.
Microsoft Flight Simulator, a low pass over a city at dusk. A graphic frame counter, added in the edit, doubles.
Split screen: frames the game drew on the left, generated frames slotted between them on the right.
The game's save file, replay timeline, and network code as three boxes; the generated frames pass beside them without connecting.
A Project Genie world, with a graphic timer counting down from sixty seconds.
Factorio. A long production line running at full speed, then stopping stage by stage from the end backwards.
Fourteen labelled tiles for the family's mechanics. All but two go grey.
The player clicks the assembler at the end of the stalled line. Far upstream, off screen, one furnace sits idle. A slow pan finds it.
The family bars, narrative and generation at the top.
Two piles of game covers: a tall one labelled "place buildings," a short one labelled "story events." A single cover slides into the gap between them.
Cities: Skylines. A district built in one go, decades later: hearses queued down the street, house after house.
Surviving Mars: a colony of domes, then a Mystery's first event window.
The ranked table of bets, sorted by priority. The top row lifts out of the table and grows to fill the frame.
Mock-up, labelled: a city view. The player right-clicks a closed hospital and picks "why?". Five short sentences appear, each with a link; clicking one scrubs a timeline back to the event it names.
A calendar flips to the bet's resolve-by date.
An animated diagram, labelled as one: two monitors showing the same strategy map. The right one carries a label: faster PC.
A clock icon over each screen. On the left the enemy cavalry turns north; on the right it holds. Two checksums appear, different. A dialog box: "Desync".
A row of technique cards; the ones that break reproducibility turn red.
A wall calendar flips to 31 December 2027. Index cards pin themselves to the date.
The first card fills the frame. Its criteria highlight clause by clause.
Two run records side by side, operator and model highlighted, different in both.
The catalog grid with the pause, placement, and tech-tree columns blank.

A re-enactment, labelled as one: several terminal windows, each an agent cataloguing a different slice of games. Their records scroll by: storytellers, production chains, mood breaks. No pause buttons.
The blank columns fill in from top to bottom; the pause column ends up the fullest on the board.
